walkthroughs.body_html:
An Introduction to Christian Ethics — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

An Introduction to Christian Ethics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with An Introduction to Christian Ethics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the second formulation about?
options: Universalisability
Humanity as end
Kingdom of ends
Good will

mcqs.q: What is the central principle of situation ethics?
options: You should do whatever feels right in the moment.
The only intrinsically good thing is agape love; rules can be broken if doing so produces the most loving outcome in the situation.
Situation ethics says rules should always be followed.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.

mcqs.q: What does utilitarianism say is right action?
options: Whatever makes you personally happy is the right thing to do.
The action that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by consequences, not intentions or rules.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
Situation ethics says rules should always be followed.

mcqs.q: What does Kant's categorical imperative require?
options: Treat others how you would like to be treated.
Do whatever your conscience tells you to do.
Acting only on maxims you could will to be universal laws, and treating people as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.

options: 4 formulations
3 formulations
1 formulations

mcqs.q: Jesus' summary of the law (Mark 12:29-31) commands:
options: love of God with all one's heart and love of neighbour as oneself
obedience to the food laws and circumcision
non-resistance to the Roman authorities
tithing and temple sacrifice

mcqs.q: Divine command theory holds that actions are right because:
options: God commands them
they maximise happiness
they accord with human nature's telos
they can be universalised without contradiction

mcqs.q: Kant's example of the shopkeeper who is honest only to keep his customers shows that:
options: acting in accordance with duty is not the same as acting from duty
honesty always maximises profit
shopkeepers cannot act morally
consequences determine moral worth

mcqs.q: Agape differs from eros in that agape is:
options: unconditional, self-giving love willed for the other's sake
romantic desire for another person
affection between family members only
love of God for the sake of reward
